source_text: Πάν τως δὲ καὶ εἴ τι τούτων μέσον, συναπεγενήθη τοῖς πέρασιν. Ὥστε κἂν μηδὲν εἴπῃ περὶ τῶν στοιχείων, πυρὸς, καὶ ὕδατος, καὶ ἀέρος, ἀλλὰ σὺ τῇ παρὰ σαυτοῦ συνέσει νόει, πρῶτον μὲν ὅτι πάντα ἐν πᾶσι μέμικται, καὶ ἐν γῇ εὑρήσεις καὶ ὕδωρ, καὶ ἀέρα, καὶ πῦρ, εἴγε ἐκ λίθων μὲν πῦρ ἐξάλλεται, ἐκ σιδήρου δὲ, ὃς καὶ αὐτὸς ἀπὸ γῆς ἔχει τὴν γένεσιν, πῦρ ἄφθονον ἐν ταῖς παρατρίψεσι πέφυκεν ἀπολάμπειν. Ὃ καὶ θαυμάσαι ἄξιον, πῶς ἐν μὲν τοῖς σώμασιν ὑπάρχον τὸ πῦρ, ἀβλαβῶς ἐμφωλεύει· προκληθὲν δὲ ἐπὶ τὸ ἔξω, δαπανητικόν ἐστι τῶν φυλασσόντων τέως. Τὴν δὲ τοῦ ὕδατος φύσιν ἐνυπάρχουσαν τῇ γῇ οἱ φρεωρύχοι δεικνύουσι· καὶ τὴν τοῦ ἀέρος οἱ ἀπὸ νενοτισμένης αὐτῆς ἀτμοὶ ὑπὸ ἡλίου θαλφθείσης ἀναπεμπόμενοι. Ἔπειτα μέντοι καὶ εἰ φύσει τὸν ἄνω τόπον ὁ οὐρανὸς ἐπέχει, ἡ δὲ γῆ τὸ κατώτατόν ἐστι· διότι ἐπὶ μὲν τὸν οὐρανὸν τὰ κοῦφα φέρεται, ἐπὶ δὲ τὴν γῆν τὰ βαρέα πέφυκε καταρρέπειν, ἐναντιώτατα δὲ ἀλλήλοις, τὸ ἄνω καὶ τὸ κάτω· ὁ τῶν πλεῖστον διεστώτων κατὰ τὴν φύσιν ἐπιμνησθεὶς, καὶ τὰ τὴν μέσην τούτοις ἐκπληροῦντα χώραν συνεκδοχικῶς παρεσήμανεν. Ὥστε μὴ ζήτει τὴν τῶν καθ' ἕκαστον ἐπεξήγησιν, ἀλλὰ τὰ σιωπηθέντα νόει διὰ τῶν δηλωθέντων. 1.8 Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν. Ἡ περὶ τῆς οὐσίας ἔρευνα ἑκάστου τῶν ὄντων, ἢ τῶν κατὰ θεωρίαν ὑποπιπτόντων ἡμῖν, ἢ τῶν προκειμένων ἡμῶν τῇ αἰσθήσει, μακρὸν καὶ ἀπηρτημένον λόγον ἐπεισάγει τῇ ἐξηγήσει, ὡς πλείονας ἐν τῇ περὶ τοῦ προβλήματος τούτου σκέψει καταναλίσκεσθαι λόγους τῶν λοιπῶν, ὅσα ἐνδέχεται ῥηθῆναι περὶ ἑκάστου τῶν ζητουμένων· πρὸς τὸ, μηδὲ προύργου τι εἶναι εἰς τὴν τῆς Ἐκκλησίας οἰκοδομὴν τὸ περὶ ταῦτα κατασχολεῖσθαι. Ἀλλὰ περὶ μὲν τῆς οὐσίας τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἀρκούμεθα τοῖς παρὰ τοῦ Ἡσαΐου εἰρημένοις· ὃς ἐν ἰδιωτικοῖς ῥήμασιν ἱκανὴν ἡμῖν τῆς φύσεως αὐτοῦ τὴν διάνοιαν ἐνεποίησεν, εἰπών· Ὁ στερεώσας τὸν οὐρανὸν ὡσεὶ καπνόν· τουτέστι, λεπτὴν φύσιν καὶ οὐ στερεὰν οὐδὲ παχεῖαν εἰς τὴν τοῦ οὐρανοῦ σύστασιν οὐσιώσας. Καὶ περὶ τοῦ σχήματος δὲ ἱκανὰ ἡμῖν τὰ παρ' αὐτοῦ, εἰπόντος ἐν δοξολογίᾳ Θεοῦ· Ὁ στήσας τὸν οὐρανὸν ὡσεὶ καμάραν. Τὰ αὐτὰ δὲ ταῦτα καὶ περὶ τῆς γῆς συμβουλεύωμεν ἑαυτοῖς, μὴ πολυπραγμονεῖν αὐτῆς τὴν οὐσίαν ἥτις ποτέ ἐστι, μηδὲ κατατρίβεσθαι τοῖς λογισμοῖς αὐτὸ τὸ ὑποκεί μενον ἐκζητοῦντας, μηδὲ ζητεῖν τινα φύσιν ἔρημον ποιοτήτων, ἄποιον ὑπάρχουσαν τῷ ἑαυτῆς λόγῳ, ἀλλ' εὖ εἰδέναι, ὅτι πάντα τὰ περὶ αὐτὴν θεωρούμενα εἰς τὸν τοῦ εἶναι κατατέτακται λόγον, συμπληρωτικὰ τῆς οὐσίας ὑπάρχοντα. Εἰς οὐδὲν γὰρ καταλήξεις, ἑκάστην τῶν ἐνυπαρχουσῶν αὐτῇ ποιοτήτων ὑπεξαιρεῖσθαι τῷ λόγῳ πειρώμενος. Ἐὰν γὰρ ἀποστήσῃς τὸ μέλαν, τὸ ψυχρὸν, τὸ βαρὺ, τὸ πυκνὸν, τὰς κατὰ γεῦσιν ἐνυπαρχούσας αὐτῇ ποιότητας, ἢ εἴ τινες ἄλλαι περὶ αὐτὴν θεωροῦνται, οὐδὲν ἔσται τὸ ὑποκείμενον. Ταῦτά τε οὖν καταλιπόντα σε, μηδὲ ἐκεῖνο ζητεῖν παραινῶ, ἐπὶ τίνος ἕστηκεν. Ἰλιγγιάσει γὰρ καὶ οὕτως ἡ διάνοια, πρὸς οὐδὲν ὁμολογούμενον πέρας διεξιόντος τοῦ λογισμοῦ.
thought_title: The extremes imply the middle; do not probe the substance of heaven or earth
orientation: Basil is expounding Genesis 1:1, arguing that by naming heaven and earth Moses indicated all that lies between them, and he now warns against inquiring into the substance of heaven and earth.
pass_a_gloss: And certainly also if anything is between these, it came into being together with the extremes. So that even if he says nothing about the elements, fire, and water, and air, but you by your own understanding understand, first that all things are mixed in all things, and in earth you will find both water, and air, and fire, if indeed from stones fire leaps out, and from iron, which itself also has its origin from earth, abundant fire in friction is wont to flash forth. Which also is worthy of wonder, how fire existing in bodies lurks harmlessly; but when called out to the outside, it is destructive of those guarding it for a time. And the nature of water existing in the earth the well-diggers show; and the nature of air the vapors from it when moistened and warmed by the sun sent up. Then further also if by nature heaven occupies the upper place, and the earth is the lowest; because to heaven the light things are borne, and to the earth the heavy things are wont to sink down, and most opposite to each other are the up and the down; the one who mentioned the things most distant according to nature also indicated by synecdoche the things filling the middle space between these. So that do not seek the detailed explanation of each individual thing, but understand the things passed over in silence through the things declared. 1.8 In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth. The inquiry about the substance of each of the things that exist, either of those falling under our contemplation, or of those set before our sense, introduces a long and detached discourse into the exposition, so that more words are consumed in the examination of this problem than of the rest, as many as can be said about each of the things investigated; to the point that it is not even useful for the building up of the Church to busy oneself about these things. But concerning the substance of heaven we are content with the things said by Isaiah; who in simple words produced in us an adequate understanding of its nature, saying: He who made firm the heaven as smoke; that is, he gave substance to a fine nature and not a solid nor thick one for the constitution of the heaven. And concerning its shape also adequate for us are the things from him, who said in doxology of God: He who set the heaven as a vault. And these same things also concerning the earth we counsel ourselves, not to busy ourselves overmuch about its substance, whatever it ever is, nor to be worn down by reasonings seeking out the underlying thing itself, nor to seek some nature devoid of qualities, existing without quality by its own definition, but to know well, that all the things observed about it are ordered to the definition of being, being completions of the substance. For you will arrive at nothing, trying by reason to remove each of the qualities existing in it. For if you take away the black, the cold, the heavy, the dense, the qualities according to taste existing in it, or if any others are observed about it, the underlying thing will be nothing. Therefore leaving these things, I advise you not to seek that either, on what it stands. For the mind will grow dizzy in this way too, the reasoning passing through to no agreed end.

choices.english: came into being together with the extremes
choices.why: The compound verb with συν- expresses simultaneous coming into being with the named extremes; 'extremes' renders πέρασιν as the two endpoints of the universe Basil has just named.
rejected: came to be along with the boundaries

choices.english: in friction is wont to flash forth
choices.why: πέφυκεν indicates natural tendency, and ἀπολάμπειν suggests sudden flashing out, fitting the image of fire struck from iron.
rejected: is accustomed to gleam in friction

choices.english: it is destructive of those guarding it for a time
choices.why: δαπανητικόν means consuming or destructive; φυλασσόντων τέως preserves the temporal nuance that bodies guard the fire only for a while before it consumes them.
rejected: it consumes what previously protected it
it is ruinous to its former guardians

choices.why: The adverb συνεκδοχικῶς is a technical rhetorical term; rendering it as 'by synecdoche' preserves Basil's precise claim that naming the extremes implies the middle.

choices.term: λεπτὴν φύσιν καὶ οὐ στερεὰν οὐδὲ παχεῖαν
choices.english: a fine nature and not a solid nor thick one
choices.why: λεπτὴν means fine or subtle, contrasted with στερεὰν (solid) and παχεῖαν (thick); the three adjectives map the physical qualities Basil attributes to heaven.
rejected: a thin nature and not a firm nor dense one
a subtle substance, neither solid nor coarse

choices.english: existing without quality by its own definition
choices.why: ἄποιον is the technical philosophical term 'without quality'; τῷ ἑαυτῆς λόγῳ means by its own account or definition, preserving the philosophical register Basil is rejecting.
rejected: devoid of qualities according to its own principle

bible_refs.note: Ὁ στερεώσας τὸν οὐρανὸν ὡσεὶ καπνόν (He who made firm the heaven as smoke); Basil quotes this as from Isaiah.
Ὁ στήσας τὸν οὐρανὸν ὡσεὶ καμάραν (He who set the heaven as a vault); Basil cites this as from Isaiah in doxology of God.

pass_b_english: And certainly whatever lies between these two also came into being together with the extremes. So even if Moses says nothing about the elements—fire, water, and air—you should understand by your own reasoning, first, that all things are mixed with all things. In earth you will find water, air, and fire: fire leaps out from stones, and from iron—which itself has its origin from the earth—abundant fire is wont to flash forth in friction. This is worth marveling at: fire exists within bodies and lurks there without harm, but once it is called outside, it is destructive of those guarding it for a time. Well-diggers show that the nature of water is present in the earth, and the vapors rising from earth moistened and warmed by the sun show the presence of air. Then further, if heaven by nature occupies the upper region and the earth is the lowest—because light things are carried toward heaven, while heavy things naturally sink down toward the earth, and up and down are most opposite to each other—then the one who mentioned the things most distant from each other by nature also indicated by synecdoche the things that fill the space between them. So do not seek an explanation of each individual thing, but understand what was passed over in silence through what was spoken.

“In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth.” The investigation of the substance of each existing thing—whether of those that fall under our contemplation or of those set before our senses—would introduce a long and detached discourse into the exposition, so that more words would be consumed in examining this problem than all the rest that can be said about each of the questions. And this would be of no benefit for the building up of the Church. But concerning the substance of heaven, we are satisfied with what Isaiah said. In simple words he gave us an adequate understanding of its nature when he said, “He who made firm the heaven as smoke” (Isaiah 40:22)—that is, he gave the heaven a fine nature for its composition, not a solid nor thick one. And concerning its shape, what he said is sufficient for us, when he said in praise of God, “He who set the heaven as a vault” (Isaiah 40:22). Let us give ourselves the same counsel concerning the earth: not to busy ourselves overmuch with its substance, whatever it may be, nor to wear ourselves out with reasonings by seeking out the underlying reality itself, nor to seek some nature devoid of qualities, existing without quality by its own definition. Rather, we should know well that everything observed about the earth is ordered toward the principle of its being, and these things complete its substance. For you will arrive at nothing if you try by reasoning to strip away each of the qualities that exist in it. If you remove the black, the cold, the heavy, the dense, the qualities of taste that exist in it, or any others that are observed about it, there will be no underlying reality left. So I urge you to leave these questions aside, and not to seek on what the earth stands. For the mind will grow dizzy this way too, as the reasoning proceeds toward no agreed-upon end.

last_rejected.quote: those guarding it for a time
last_rejected.why: τέως means 'for the present' or 'for now,' not 'for a time' in the sense of a duration; but more critically, φυλασσόντων τέως means 'those guarding it for now/presently,' i.e., the bodies containing it. The English 'for a time' is vague. Actually, re-reading: 'destructive of those guarding it for a time'—this suggests the fire destroys those who guard it temporarily. But τέως means 'for the present, for now,' indicating the bodies currently containing it. The English slightly misrepresents: 'those guarding it for a time' implies people guarding fire for a limited period, but the Greek means 'those currently containing/guarding it' (i.e., the bodies). This is a mistranslation of τέως.
last_rejected.fix: destructive of those that now contain it
last_rejected.ruling: τέως means 'for the present/for now'; 'for a time' is within acceptable range and does not mislead the reader.

last_rejected.quote: existing without quality by its own definition
last_rejected.why: τῷ ἑαυτῆς λόγῳ means 'by its own account/ratio/principle,' not 'by its own definition.' λόγος here means 'account, principle, formula,' not 'definition' in the technical sense. 'By its own definition' is a modern philosophical imposition. The Greek means 'existing without quality according to its own principle/account.'
last_rejected.fix: existing without quality by its own principle
last_rejected.ruling: λόγος can mean 'definition'; 'by its own definition' is within the word's normal range and not misleading.

last_rejected.why: The Greek says 'being complementary/completive of the substance,' i.e., 'contributing to completing the substance.' The English 'these things complete its substance' is too strong—'complete' suggests they finish or fully constitute it, whereas συμπληρωτικά means 'contributing to the completion, complementary.' The qualities don't complete the substance on their own; they are complementary to it.
last_rejected.fix: contributing to the completion of its substance
last_rejected.ruling: συμπληρωτικά means 'completing'; 'complete its substance' is within range, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.why: τὸ μέλαν means 'the black' as a noun ('blackness'), but in context of earth's qualities, this refers to 'the dark(color)' or 'blackness.' The English 'the black' is grammatically odd but conveys the meaning. However, 'black' as a quality of earth is strange—earth is typically brown. But the Greek says μέλαν, 'black/dark.' This is what the source says. Not an error.
last_rejected.ruling: Self-reported as not an error; τὸ μέλαν = 'the black,' accurately rendered.

last_rejected.quote: And this would be of no benefit
last_rejected.source_quote: πρὸς τὸ, μηδὲ προύργου τι εἶναι
last_rejected.why: The English adds 'And this would be' which interprets the syntax, but the Greek is πρὸς τὸ μηδὲ προύργου τι εἶναι—'with respect to its being of no use at all.' The English 'this would be of no benefit' captures the sense. However, the construction is purpose/result: 'so that... it would be of no use.' The English 'And this would be' changes the grammar but not the sense. Not reporting.
last_rejected.ruling: Self-reported as not an error; sense is correctly captured.

last_rejected.why: ἰδιωτικοῖς means 'of a private person, unlearned, common,' i.e., 'in plain/common language,' not 'simple' in the sense of uncomplicated. 'Simple words' is close but slightly misses the connotation of 'uneducated, non-technical' language that contrasts with philosophical jargon. 'Simple' is within range. Not reporting.
last_rejected.ruling: Self-reported as not an error; 'simple' is within range for ἰδιωτικοῖς.
